recipes.title: Install and start n8n on your own PC
recipes.keywords: n8n install npm npx start localhost 5678 node local self-hosted
recipes.goal: n8n is running on your PC and the editor is open in your browser.
recipes.plan_needed: The npm install page does not state a price. It does say npm installs are deprecated starting with n8n 3.0 and that the n8n Assistant is not available with npm installs.
before: Node.js installed. The page says n8n needs a version from 20.19 through 24.x.
A terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt).

steps.do: Check your Node.js version by running node -v in a terminal.
steps.why: n8n only supports certain Node versions.
steps.check: You see a version number between 20.19 and 24.x.

steps.do: To try n8n without installing, run npx n8n. To install it for good, run npm install n8n -g and then start it with n8n (or n8n start).
steps.why: npx is a quick test; the global install is what you keep using.
steps.check: The terminal prints that n8n is ready and keeps running. Do not close it.

steps.do: Open http://localhost:5678 in your browser.
steps.why: This is the address the page gives for the n8n editor.
steps.check: You see the n8n setup or login page.

steps.do: Create your owner account when asked, using your own email and a password you keep in your password manager.
steps.why: Your local n8n holds your credentials, so only you should sign in.
steps.check: You land on the n8n home screen.

steps.do: To update later, run npm update -g n8n in the terminal and start n8n again.
steps.why: Updates bring fixes and new nodes.
steps.check: n8n starts again and your workflows are still there.

steps.do: Remember that a service on the internet (a Vapi call, a form on your website, a GitHub hook) cannot reach localhost. For those you need a public HTTPS address, for example the tunnel option described on the npm page.
steps.why: Webhooks from outside must reach your PC.
steps.check: You know to plan a public URL before you promise a client a live webhook.

mistakes: Closing the terminal window: n8n stops and every workflow stops with it.
Using an unsupported Node.js version: the install may fail or behave oddly. Check node -v first.
Expecting webhooks from the internet to hit localhost: they cannot without a public URL or tunnel.
Using the tunnel for client production work: the page says the tunnel is for local development and testing only.
done_when: http://localhost:5678 opens the n8n editor.
You can create and save an empty workflow.
recipes.free_alternative: The npm page does not name one. n8n Cloud has a free trial per the tutorial page, but it is not the self-hosted route.
unverified: Exact wording of the owner-account setup screen was not on the page.
Whether your team's local install at C:/Users/Administrator/n8n-local differs from the plain npm route was not checked against the docs.

recipes.title: Build a simple n8n workflow
recipes.keywords: n8n workflow build automation trigger node schedule http request edit fields execute publish first workflow
recipes.goal: A working workflow that starts on a schedule, fetches data, shapes it and saves it, tested and published.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the page for the manual build. The page says the n8n Assistant is not part of npm installs, so use the manual path on a local install.
before: n8n open in your browser (see the start-local recipe).
Optional: the n8n tutorial page open beside you for the sample URL.

steps.do: In n8n open Personal, then select Create workflow. Rename the workflow and click the canvas to keep the name.
steps.why: A clear name makes it easy to find later.
steps.check: You see an empty canvas with your workflow name at the top.

steps.do: Select Add first step, then choose On a schedule. Set Trigger at Hour to 8am and close the panel.
steps.why: Every workflow needs a trigger that says when it starts.
steps.check: A schedule node appears on the canvas. Rename it so you remember what it does (the tutorial uses 'Every day at 8 AM').

steps.do: Select the + after the trigger, search for HTTP Request and add it. Paste the data URL into the URL field.
steps.why: This node fetches data from the internet.
steps.check: The node shows a URL.

steps.do: Select Execute step on the HTTP Request node.
steps.why: Testing each node as you go finds mistakes early.
steps.check: You see output data in the node panel.

steps.do: Select + again, open Data transformation, and choose Edit Fields (Set). Select Add Field, name it report, and build its Value, then select Execute step.
steps.why: This turns raw data into the exact fields you want.
steps.check: The output shows a report field with your text.

steps.do: Add a Data table node with the Insert row action. Create a new data table, add a column named report, then set Mapping Column Mode to Map Automatically.
steps.why: Saving the result proves the workflow did something useful.
steps.check: The node is connected with no red warnings.

steps.do: Select Execute under the canvas to run the whole workflow, then check Personal, then Data tables.
steps.why: A full test shows the nodes work together.
steps.check: A new row with your report appears in the table.

steps.do: Select Publish in the Canvas header and follow the prompts.
steps.why: Only a published workflow runs by itself on its trigger.
steps.check: The workflow shows as published and will run at the scheduled time.

mistakes: Skipping Execute step on each node: errors pile up and are harder to find.
Leaving the default node names: with ten nodes you will not know which is which. Rename them.
Forgetting to publish: the test run works but nothing happens at 8am.
Closing the terminal where n8n runs on your PC: scheduled runs only happen while n8n is running.
done_when: Execute produced a new row in your data table.
The workflow is published.
Every node has a clear name.
recipes.free_alternative: Self-hosted n8n on your own PC; the tutorial page does not state a cost for the manual build.
unverified: The tutorial page is written for the current n8n editor; your local version may use older labels (for example Activate instead of Publish). If a label differs, find the equivalent option.
The tutorial's Data table node was not checked against the n8n version installed on the team PCs.

recipes.title: Send replies from email into the CRM with n8n
recipes.keywords: n8n reply router replies crm hubspot email imap trigger switch classify route interested unsubscribe
recipes.goal: New email replies are sorted automatically, interested ones create or update a HubSpot contact, and you get an alert.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the node pages. HubSpot's own plan limits were not checked.
before: n8n running (see the start-local recipe).
Mailbox IMAP details for the inbox that receives replies.
A HubSpot account where you can create a service key (super admin or Developer tools access permission per the n8n page).
An SMTP account if you want an email alert.

steps.do: Create a new workflow and add the Email Trigger (IMAP) node. Under Credential to connect with, create an IMAP credential for the reply inbox.
steps.why: This node starts the workflow each time an email arrives.
steps.check: The credential saves without an error.

steps.do: In that node set Mailbox Name to the inbox you want, set Action to None (leaves emails unread) or Mark as Read, and leave Download Attachments off.
steps.why: Attachments add processing and replies rarely need them.
steps.check: Select Execute step and send yourself a test email: it shows up in the node output.

steps.do: Add a Switch node. Under Routing Rules add one rule per type of reply (for example interested, not now, unsubscribe) that checks the email text for key words.
steps.why: Each rule gets its own output so each reply type goes a different way.
steps.check: Run the test and see the email leave from the output you expected.

steps.do: In the Switch node set Fallback Output to Extra Output.
steps.why: Replies that match no rule are not lost.
steps.check: A fifth output appears for unmatched emails.

steps.do: On the interested output add a HubSpot node and choose the contact operation to create or update a contact. Create the credential with a HubSpot service key pasted into the App Token field.
steps.why: This writes the person into your CRM without typing.
steps.check: Execute step shows the contact; it then appears in HubSpot.

steps.do: Add a second HubSpot node using a deal operation if you also want a deal, and link it to the contact.
steps.why: A deal lets you track the lead through your sales stages.
steps.check: The deal appears in HubSpot.

steps.do: On the unsubscribe output, make sure that person is never contacted again: record them in your suppression list or tag the contact in HubSpot.
steps.why: Honouring opt-outs is a legal requirement for cold email in the US and UK.
steps.check: The person is marked do-not-contact somewhere you check before sending.

steps.do: Add a Send Email node (SMTP credential) with From Email, To Email, Subject and Email Format to alert yourself with the next step.
steps.why: You need to reply to hot leads quickly.
steps.check: A test alert arrives in your inbox.

steps.do: Test with several sample replies, then publish the workflow.
steps.why: Real replies are messy. Samples catch wrong routing before it matters.
steps.check: Each sample ends up in the right place and the workflow shows as published.

mistakes: Routing on one exact word: people write 'Yes, send details'. Use several key words per rule.
Pasting your HubSpot key into a note or chat: it only belongs in the n8n credential.
Not handling unsubscribe replies: ignoring them breaks CAN-SPAM and UK rules.
Marking emails as read by accident so you miss them in the inbox: choose Action None while testing.
Skipping the fallback output: odd replies vanish silently.
done_when: A test interested reply creates or updates a HubSpot contact.
A test unsubscribe reply is marked do-not-contact.
You receive the alert email.
The workflow is published.
recipes.free_alternative: n8n self-hosted with a free HubSpot account (limits not checked).
unverified: IMAP credential field names were not read (the page links to a separate page).
The exact node name 'Switch' output limit and how the Extra Output is labelled on your version.
Exact HubSpot operation wording (the page says 'Create/Update a contact'; the editor may word it differently).
HubSpot service keys were described as public beta and may change.
The existing team Reply Router in engine-c-upwork/item3-reply-router was not checked against the docs.
CAN-SPAM and UK PECR specifics were not re-fetched for this recipe.

recipes.title: Automate client intake with n8n
recipes.keywords: automation n8n intake form trigger onboarding webhook auto reply booking link ai automation new client
recipes.goal: When a new client submits your intake form, n8n sends an instant reply with next steps and a booking link, saves their details, and alerts you.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the Form Trigger page.
before: n8n running (see the start-local recipe).
A booking link (for example from Cal.com).
An SMTP account for sending the auto-reply.
A place to save details (a Data table in n8n, HubSpot, or a sheet).

steps.do: Map the client's current intake on paper first: what do they ask, what files do they collect, who needs to know.
steps.why: You can only automate a process you understand.
steps.check: You have a short list of fields and who gets notified.

steps.do: Create a workflow and add the n8n Form Trigger node. Set a Form Title.
steps.why: n8n builds the form page for you; the title is the heading people see.
steps.check: The node shows a Test URL and a Production URL.

steps.do: Under Form Elements select Add Form Element for each field. Set Element Type (use Email for the email, Textarea for notes), Field Label, Field Name and turn on Required Field where needed.
steps.why: Field Name is the key you use in later nodes.
steps.check: Select Execute Step and open the Test URL: the form shows your fields.

steps.do: Fill in the test form and submit it.
steps.why: The test data lets you map fields in the next nodes.
steps.check: The submitted values appear in the node output in the editor.

steps.do: Add a Send Email node. Fill From Email, To Email (map the submitter's email), Subject and the message with next steps and your booking link. Pick Email Format.
steps.why: An instant reply shows the client you are responsive.
steps.check: The test submission sends you an email with the booking link.

steps.do: Add a node to store the details (for example a Data table Insert row, or the HubSpot create or update contact option).
steps.why: You must not lose the lead if an email is missed.
steps.check: A new row or contact exists after a test.

steps.do: Add a Send Email node to notify yourself or your team of the new submission.
steps.why: Someone has to act on it.
steps.check: You receive the alert.

steps.do: Set Respond When on the Form Trigger. Form Is Submitted replies at once; Workflow Finishes waits for the whole workflow.
steps.why: Choose Form Is Submitted if later steps could be slow.
steps.check: The form shows its thank-you message after submit.

steps.do: Publish the workflow, then use the Production URL for the real form.
steps.why: The Test URL only works while you are testing.
steps.check: A real submission appears under the workflow's Executions tab.

mistakes: Sharing the Test URL with a client: it only works while you are listening in the editor. Use the Production URL.
Not telling people why you collect their data: add a short privacy note and link on the form.
Collecting more personal data than the job needs.
Mapping the wrong Field Name: the auto-reply goes nowhere. Test with your own email first.
Forgetting to publish after changes.
done_when: A test submission sends the auto-reply with the booking link.
The details are saved.
You get a team alert.
The workflow is published and a real submission shows in Executions.
recipes.free_alternative: Self-hosted n8n and its built-in form page.
unverified: Handling uploaded files (File element type) into storage was not researched.
A form on the client's own website would need the Webhook node or a public URL: with a local n8n the Production URL is only reachable inside your network unless a public address or tunnel is set up.
Pricing for the service (build and monthly care) is from the team's own notes, not from n8n.

recipes.title: Build an AI receptionist in Vapi
recipes.keywords: vapi voice ai receptionist assistant phone number calls booking appointment first message system prompt publish
recipes.goal: A Vapi assistant that answers a phone call as an honest AI receptionist, tested in the browser, with a phone number attached and call details sent out for the owner.
recipes.plan_needed: The Vapi pages say your first free Vapi number needs no payment method and is US, inbound only. Outbound calls need an imported number (Twilio, Telnyx or DIDWW). Prices were not on the pages: see Vapi's pricing page. Call minutes are billed by Vapi (not checked).
before: A Vapi account (dashboard.vapi.ai).
The client's business name, opening hours, services, prices they allow you to share, and common questions.
A call-recording and AI disclosure decision (see the legal basics recipe).
Optional: an n8n workflow with a Production URL for call summaries.

steps.do: Open the Vapi Dashboard and select Assistants. Select the arrow next to Create Assistant and pick a template such as Appointment Scheduler or Customer Support.
steps.why: A template gives you a first message and a system prompt to edit.
steps.check: A new assistant opens with First Message and System Prompt filled in.

steps.do: Rename the assistant (for example Receptionist).
steps.why: You will have one assistant per client.
steps.check: The new name shows in the Assistants list.

steps.do: Edit First Message so the first thing callers hear is the business name and a plain statement that this is an AI assistant, for example that they are speaking with the virtual assistant for the business.
steps.why: People should know they are talking to an AI from the first sentence.
steps.check: You hear the disclosure when you test.

steps.do: Edit the System Prompt: add business name, hours, services, FAQs, what to do when unsure (take a name and number), and a rule that the assistant never claims to be a human. Keep replies short.
steps.why: The assistant only knows what you tell it.
steps.check: The prompt contains the client's real facts and no made-up prices.

steps.do: Check the model and voice. New assistants use the Balanced preset, which sets the transcriber, model and voice together.
steps.why: The preset keeps beginners from mis-tuning settings.
steps.check: The assistant shows a preset with a voice.

steps.do: Select Talk to start a web call. Allow the browser to use your microphone.
steps.why: Testing in the browser costs nothing extra to set up and finds prompt problems.
steps.check: You can talk to the assistant and it greets you with the AI disclosure.

steps.do: Test the hard cases: a caller asks for the owner, asks something not in the prompt, asks 'Am I talking to a real person?', asks to book.
steps.why: Real callers will do all of these.
steps.check: The assistant stays honest (admits it is an AI) and takes a message when it cannot answer.

steps.do: Select Publish, review the changes, select Next, review version and traffic settings, then select Publish.
steps.why: Until you publish, changes stay as a draft and do not affect real calls.
steps.check: A new assistant version exists.

steps.do: Get a phone number: create the free Vapi number in the dashboard (US area code, inbound calls only) or import one from a provider.
steps.why: The number is what callers dial.
steps.check: The number appears in Phone Numbers.

steps.do: Attach the assistant to the phone number so inbound calls use it, then call the number from your phone.
steps.why: This links the number to the assistant.
steps.check: Your phone call is answered by your assistant.

steps.do: Under the assistant's Advanced tab, find Webhook Server and enter the Server URL of an n8n Production URL so you can receive the end-of-call report (it carries the transcript, messages and recording URLs).
steps.why: Lets n8n send the owner a call summary.
steps.check: After a test call a request shows in the n8n workflow's Executions tab.

steps.do: For client forwarding of missed calls to your Vapi number: set this up with the client's phone provider (call forwarding). Check the provider's own help for how.
steps.why: The client keeps their number and forwards only missed calls.
steps.check: A missed call to the client's number is answered by the assistant.

mistakes: Letting the assistant pretend to be human: it is dishonest and can create legal risk. State it is an AI and answer honestly if asked.
Putting invented prices, hours or promises in the prompt: use only facts the client approved.
Forgetting Publish: your edits do not reach real calls.
Using a free Vapi number for outbound calls: free numbers are inbound only.
Not telling callers about recording: see the legal basics recipe.
Using the n8n Test URL as the Server URL: use the Production URL of a published workflow.
done_when: A web test call works and the assistant says it is an AI.
The assistant is published.
A real call to the number reaches the assistant.
A test call produced a report in n8n (if you set that up).
recipes.free_alternative: The Vapi free number needs no payment method; call usage costs were not stated on the pages.
unverified: How to turn recording on or off per assistant was not found on the pages fetched. Check the assistant settings in the dashboard.
The exact steps to attach an assistant to a number in the Dashboard UI (the page only says to set an assistantId).
Whether the end-of-call report includes a summary field: the events page lists transcript, messages and recording only, and does not show how to enable serverMessages in the Dashboard.
How to voice-select or change voice within the Balanced preset in the Dashboard.
Call forwarding steps depend on the client's phone carrier.
Whether a free Vapi number is available outside the US or for UK clients.

recipes.title: Legal basics for an AI phone receptionist (US and UK)
recipes.keywords: vapi ai receptionist legal disclosure recording consent two party tcpa fcc ico gdpr impersonate human ai voice calls compliance
recipes.goal: You know the basic rules to follow before putting an AI voice assistant on a client's phone line, and your prompt and greeting follow them.
recipes.plan_needed: Not applicable. This is general information from regulator pages, not legal advice: have the client check with a lawyer for their state or country.
before: Know where the client and their callers are (US state, UK).
Know if calls are inbound (callers phone the client) or outbound (the assistant phones people).

steps.do: Tell callers right at the start that they are speaking to an AI assistant. Put it in the First Message.
steps.why: The FTC says there is no AI exemption from deception laws, and pretending to be human can be deceptive. Vapi's pages do not set a disclosure rule, so this is your own safe practice.
steps.check: A test call opens with a clear AI statement.

steps.do: Add a rule in the System Prompt: never say or imply you are a human, and if asked, say you are an AI assistant.
steps.why: The assistant must stay honest when asked directly.
steps.check: Ask it 'Are you a real person?' in a test call and it says it is an AI.

steps.do: Do not use a cloned voice of a real person without their written permission, and never present the assistant as a named real employee.
steps.why: The FTC has acted on impersonation, and proposed extending its rule to individuals (status not confirmed).
steps.check: The assistant uses a stock voice and a role name such as 'virtual assistant'.

steps.do: If you record calls (Vapi records calls and stores transcripts by default per its own HIPAA page), tell callers at the start that the call is recorded and why.
steps.why: UK ICO guidance says people should be told when calls are recorded and why. A recorded message is good practice.
steps.check: The greeting includes a short recording notice, and a privacy page link is available.

steps.do: For US clients, check state law. The FCC says federal law generally follows one-party consent but states vary and some need all parties to agree. If any caller could be in an all-party state, announce recording and continue only if they stay on the line.
steps.why: Recording without the required consent can break state law.
steps.check: You wrote down the state rules the client must follow, or used a notice for all calls.

steps.do: Do not use the assistant for outbound calls to people who have not agreed. The FCC ruling (Feb 2024) treats AI-generated voices as an artificial voice under the TCPA, which needs the called person's prior consent, and written consent for marketing.
steps.why: Unsolicited AI robocalls are illegal in the US and can bring fines and lawsuits.
steps.check: Your plan only covers inbound receptionist calls for now.

steps.do: Keep call data safe: only the client and you see recordings and transcripts, keep them no longer than needed, and give people a way to ask for deletion.
steps.why: UK GDPR needs fairness, transparency and a lawful basis for personal data.
steps.check: A short retention rule is written in the client's service agreement.

steps.do: Do not collect payment card numbers, health details or other sensitive data by voice unless the client has a compliant setup.
steps.why: Vapi's HIPAA page covers health data separately and says do not put protected health information through the wrong parts of the platform.
steps.check: The prompt tells the assistant to refuse sensitive details and to hand off to a person.

mistakes: Thinking the AI disclosure is optional because Vapi does not demand it.
Assuming one rule covers every US state: recording consent differs by state.
Using the receptionist to phone leads who never agreed to be called.
Using a real person's voice without permission.
Promising clients that you are giving legal advice: you are not. They should confirm with a lawyer.
done_when: The greeting says it is an AI (and that calls may be recorded, if they are).
The prompt forbids pretending to be human.
The client has been told the recording and data rules in writing.
No outbound calling without consent.
recipes.free_alternative: The FCC and ICO pages listed below are free.
unverified: Whether the FCC's proposal to require AI disclosure at the start of calls has been finalised (an NPRM, FCC 24-84, was proposed; final status not confirmed).
Whether any US state or UK rule currently requires an AI disclosure on inbound calls was not confirmed on an official page.

The ICO page quoted is about monitoring workers; the ICO's separate rules on recording calls for businesses were not found as a single page. The UK Investigatory Powers and Telecoms 'lawful business practice' rules were not checked.
The current list of US all-party-consent states: the FCC page cites an older count, check current state law.
The FTC impersonation rule extension to individuals was only proposed in the sources found.
Nigerian data protection law (NDPA) was not researched.

recipes.title: Connect Cal.com booking to the AI receptionist
recipes.keywords: cal.com cal booking calendar availability voice ai vapi api key event type slots book appointment n8n
recipes.goal: A Cal.com event type with sensible length and buffers, an API key, and a way for the Vapi assistant to check free times and book through your n8n workflow.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the pages fetched. Vapi has no built-in Cal.com integration on its integrations page, so this uses a Function tool or API Request tool and a small n8n workflow.
before: A Cal.com account with your calendar connected.
A Vapi assistant (see the receptionist recipe).
An n8n workflow with a published Production URL reachable from the internet.
A safe place for the Cal.com API key (an n8n credential, not the prompt).

steps.do: In Cal.com create an event type for the call or visit you want booked. Set the title and the length in minutes (these are in the Basics tab per Cal.com's help).
steps.why: The assistant books this event type.
steps.check: The event type shows in your list and its booking page opens.

steps.do: Open the event type's Limits & buffers tab and choose a before-event or after-event buffer, then click Update.
steps.why: Buffers stop back-to-back bookings.
steps.check: The change saves.

steps.do: Set the event's availability (days and hours) so only times the client really works are offered.
steps.why: The assistant will offer whatever Cal.com shows as free.
steps.check: The public booking page only shows the right hours.

steps.do: Create an API key in Cal.com under Settings, then Security.
steps.why: The key lets n8n check slots and create bookings.
steps.check: You see the key once. Copy it into an n8n credential, not into chat or the prompt.

steps.do: Note the event type ID. In n8n add an HTTP Request node that calls Cal.com's get-slots endpoint (GET /v2/slots) with eventTypeId, start and end (UTC), an Authorization Bearer header, and the cal-api-version header the page names.
steps.why: This returns the free times to read to the caller.
steps.check: Execute step returns a list of dates and start times, or an empty object when nothing is free.

steps.do: Add a second HTTP Request node that calls POST /v2/bookings with start (UTC), attendee name, time zone and email, and eventTypeId. Send the cal-api-version header the booking page names.
steps.why: This books the slot.
steps.check: A test booking shows in Cal.com and the attendee receives the invite.

steps.do: Put a Webhook node at the start (Respond set to Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node) and a Respond to Webhook node at the end, then Publish and copy the Production URL.
steps.why: Vapi needs a JSON answer back. The Test URL does not work for Vapi.
steps.check: Calling the Production URL from a test returns JSON.

steps.do: In Vapi open Tools, then Create Tool, choose Function tool, name it (for example check_availability), set its parameters and paste the n8n Production URL as the Server URL. Make a second tool for booking.
steps.why: Vapi has no built-in Cal.com integration, so a Function tool is the documented route for services it does not cover.
steps.check: Using Test on the tool returns a response.

steps.do: Open the assistant, go to the Tools tab, select Add Tool and add both tools, then save. Update the System Prompt: confirm name, date and time back to the caller and never confirm a booking after a tool error.
steps.why: The assistant must know when to call each tool.
steps.check: In a Talk web call the assistant offers real free times.

steps.do: Test a full booking on a sandbox calendar, then check the Cal.com booking and the invite email. Publish the assistant.
steps.why: End-to-end testing proves it works before a client relies on it.
steps.check: The booking appears in Cal.com and the caller hears a correct confirmation.

mistakes: Missing or wrong cal-api-version header: the API falls back to an older version and behaves differently.
Sending local times where Cal.com expects UTC: bookings land at the wrong hour. Send the time zone too.
Putting the API key in the Vapi prompt or a public place: keep it in an n8n credential.
Using the n8n Test URL in Vapi: only the published Production URL works.
Testing on the client's real calendar: use a sandbox calendar first.
Hitting rate limits: Cal.com says API keys default to 120 requests per minute.
done_when: The assistant offers real free times from Cal.com.
A test booking appears in Cal.com with an invite.
The API key is stored only in n8n.
The assistant says the booking was confirmed only after a success.
recipes.free_alternative: A simpler fallback: have the assistant read out your Cal.com booking link by text or email instead of booking live. Whether Cal.com's free plan covers API use was not stated on the pages.
unverified: The Cal.com create-event-type help page returned 404; the Basics tab and the availability tab names come from search snippets and the live Cal.com UI may differ.
The cal-api-version values differ between endpoints (slots page said 2024-09-04, bookings 2026-02-25): confirm in the current API reference before building.
Whether the slots endpoint takes eventTypeId or username plus event slug in your version (sources disagreed).
How to attach an Authorization header on a Vapi Function tool: the page does not describe a headers field, which is why the key stays in n8n.
Whether Cal.com has a Vapi-specific guide or a Cal.com MCP option: none found on Vapi's pages.
Cal.com plan limits for API use.

recipes.title: Find local businesses and their websites
recipes.keywords: find leads companies businesses local google maps search list build table movers agencies
recipes.goal: A Clay table of local businesses with name, website and contact details for one niche and one area.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the pages found. Clay shows a credit cost for each run, so check it before you run.
before: A Clay account and an empty workspace.
One business type (for example 'moving company') and one city or area.
Read the recipe apollo-email-compliance before you email anyone you find.

recipes.title: Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC for a sending domain
recipes.keywords: spf dkim dmarc dns txt record sending domain authentication google workspace deliverability _dmarc selector
recipes.goal: Your sending domain has SPF, DKIM and DMARC records published, so Gmail and Yahoo can verify your emails really come from you.
recipes.time: about 45 minutes, plus up to 48 hours for DNS to update
recipes.plan_needed: The Google pages describe Google Workspace mailboxes. Other mailbox providers (Microsoft 365, Zoho and so on) have their own help pages with their own record values; the Google pages do not cover them.
before: A domain you control and access to its DNS settings (where you buy or host the domain).
A mailbox provider already set up for that domain. These steps use Google Workspace as the example.
Super admin access in the Google Admin console (needed for DKIM).
A free group or shared mailbox on the same domain to receive DMARC reports (do not use a personal inbox).
Your list of every tool that sends email as this domain (for example Google Workspace and your outreach tool).

steps.do: Write down every service that sends email using this domain.
steps.why: SPF must list all of them, or mail from unlisted senders is more likely to be marked as spam.
steps.check: You have a short list, for example: Google Workspace only.

steps.do: Write your SPF record. For Google Workspace only it is: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all. For more senders, add one include: for each, for example v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:amazonses.com ~all.
steps.why: SPF tells receiving servers which servers may send for your domain. Google says use up to 10 include tags in total.
steps.check: You have one line that starts with v=spf1 and ends with ~all.

steps.do: At your DNS host, add a TXT record. Type: TXT. Host: @ (for the main domain) or the subdomain name. Value: your SPF line. Keep only one SPF record per domain or subdomain.
steps.why: SPF is published as a TXT record in DNS. Some hosts want the value wrapped in quotes, so check your host's help.
steps.check: The record shows in your DNS list. Google says SPF can take up to 48 hours to start working.

steps.do: In the Google Admin console go to Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail and open Authenticate email. Select your domain and click Generate New Record.
steps.why: DKIM signs each email so it cannot be faked. Google generates the key for you.
steps.check: A DKIM host name and a long value are shown on screen.

steps.do: Choose key length 2048 if your DNS host supports it, otherwise 1024. Keep the default selector google unless your domain already uses it. Click Generate and copy the values.
steps.why: Google recommends 2048 where possible. Google's sender guidelines require at least 1024 bits.
steps.check: You copied a host name like google._domainkey and a value starting with v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=.

steps.do: At your DNS host, add a TXT record with host name google._domainkey (selector followed by ._domainkey) and the copied value. Save.
steps.why: Receiving servers look up this record to check your signature.
steps.check: The record is saved. If your host rejects it as too long, check its TXT length limit. DNS changes can take up to 48 hours.

steps.do: Wait until the DKIM record is live, then return to Authenticate email, select the domain and click Start authentication.
steps.why: Turning DKIM on before the DNS record exists makes it fail.
steps.check: Status says Authenticating email with DKIM.

steps.do: Wait about 48 hours after SPF and DKIM are on, then create your DMARC record: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:your-reports-address@yourdomain.com
steps.why: DMARC needs SPF or DKIM already working. Google suggests starting with p=none to only monitor, then moving to quarantine and later reject once you trust the results.
steps.check: You have one line starting v=DMARC1 with p= second and an rua address you can read.

steps.do: At your DNS host add a TXT record with host name _dmarc (that is _dmarc.yourdomain.com) and your DMARC line as the value.
steps.why: DMARC is looked up at _dmarc on your domain. Some hosts add the domain name for you, so check the final entry.
steps.check: The record appears in your DNS list under _dmarc.

steps.do: Send a test email to a Gmail address that is not your own sending address. In Gmail open the message, choose Show original and look at Authentication-Results. Also run your domain through a free online DMARC checker.
steps.why: This proves the records work in real mail. Sending to yourself will not verify DKIM.
steps.check: You see SPF and DKIM as pass, and the checker finds a valid DMARC record.

mistakes: Two SPF records on one domain. Keep one SPF record per domain or subdomain and add more senders into that one line.
Clicking Start authentication before the DKIM TXT record is saved in DNS.
Using a personal inbox for DMARC reports. Reports can arrive in large volumes, so use a group or dedicated mailbox.
Jumping straight to a strict DMARC policy. Start at p=none and tighten only when everything legitimate passes.
Forgetting that every domain and subdomain you send from needs its own records.
done_when: SPF, DKIM and DMARC TXT records are all published for the sending domain.
Gmail Show original shows SPF and DKIM passing for a test email.
A DMARC checker confirms the _dmarc record is valid.
recipes.free_alternative: Adding DNS records and using Show original and an online DMARC checker are free. You only pay for the domain and mailboxes themselves.
unverified: Exact DNS screens differ by registrar and were not checked; the recipe says 'your DNS host'.
Records for mailbox providers other than Google Workspace were not researched.
Instantly's help page says its Test domain setup option can check these records; that option is mentioned in the Instantly inbox recipe.

steps.do: Leave the default warm-up settings for a new account. The default is increase by 1 per day, daily warmup limit 10 and reply rate 30%. Do not turn on Disable slow warmup for a new account.
steps.why: Instantly says keep new accounts at about 10 warm-up emails a day and slow warm-up is only for already-warmed accounts.
steps.check: In the account Settings the Warmup settings show those values.

steps.do: Optionally turn on Weekdays only in the warm-up settings.
steps.why: It sends warm-up emails Monday to Friday only.
steps.check: The setting shows as on.

steps.do: Check warm-up daily for the first week: click the account and open the Warmup tab in Account Details.
steps.why: You want proof that warm-up emails are really being sent and received.
steps.check: You see warm-up emails sent and received and a Saved from spam count for the past 7 days.

steps.do: Wait at least 2 weeks (3 weeks for Airmail accounts) before using the inbox in a campaign. Also wait until the Health score column shows above 90 percent.
steps.why: Instantly gives both rules: warm-up length and health score above 90.
steps.check: Both are true: enough days passed and Health score is above 90 percent.

steps.do: When the inbox goes into a campaign, keep sending low (see the campaign recipe), and leave warm-up on.
steps.why: Instantly's own guidance is about 30 campaign emails per account per day.
steps.check: The inbox keeps a good health score while the campaign runs.

mistakes: Sending cold email from your main business domain. Use a separate sending domain so a problem cannot harm your main email.
Starting campaigns on day 1. Warm up first (Instantly says pre-warmed accounts bought from Instantly can start on day 1).
Turning on Disable slow warmup for a new account.
Reading the health score as campaign performance. It only measures warm-up emails landing in inbox versus spam, not your real campaign emails.
Warm-up emails landing in spam in the first days. Instantly says this is normal for new accounts and improves over time.
done_when: Each inbox shows connected in Email Accounts with a coloured flame.
Test domain setup finds no missing records.
At least 2 weeks have passed and Health score is above 90 percent.
recipes.free_alternative: The Instantly 14-day free trial warms up 2 accounts per its help page. Connecting a mailbox you already own costs nothing extra.
unverified: The detailed click path for connecting a Google or Microsoft account was not on the fetched page (it links to separate articles).
Whether a separate sending domain is required by Instantly is not stated; it is common deliverability practice.
Instantly blog posts mention longer 4 to 6 week warm-up timelines; the help centre says at least 2 weeks.
Current plan prices were not checked.

recipes.title: Launch an Instantly campaign from a CSV
recipes.keywords: instantly campaign launch sequence upload leads csv steps schedule send variables unsubscribe daily limit
recipes.goal: A cold email campaign with 3 to 4 short steps is live in Instantly, sending a small number of emails per day from warmed inboxes.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the page for basic campaigns. Some settings are plan limited: the help says Prioritize New Leads needs the Hyper Growth or Light Speed plan, and Limit emails per company needs Hyper Growth or higher.
before: At least one connected, warmed inbox (see the inbox recipe).
A CSV of leads whose emails are already verified, with columns such as email, first name, company name, and a personalization line.
A lawful reason to email each person and a way for them to opt out (see the GTM overview recipe).
A physical postal address for your email footer if you are emailing US recipients.

steps.do: Open the Engage dashboard and click + Create New (top right).
steps.why: This starts a new campaign.
steps.check: The new campaign builder opens.

steps.do: In the Leads section choose Import a CSV file. Map each column: Email is required, and Instantly offers First name, Last name, Job title, Company name, Personalization, Phone, Website, Location and LinkedIn. Use Do Not Import for columns you do not need.
steps.why: Mapped columns become variables you can use in your copy.
steps.check: Every column shows a mapping and the lead count matches your file.

steps.do: For extra data (for example a Country column) map it as a Custom variable. In copy you write it as {{columnName}}. Do not name it similar to a predefined variable.
steps.why: Custom variables let you personalise beyond the standard fields.
steps.check: The custom variable is listed and shows in the variable picker.

steps.do: In the Editors section write step 1 yourself: short, plain text, one clear question. Insert variables with the variable option in the bottom toolbar (for the subject line use the bolt icon).
steps.why: Instantly recommends a maximum of 3 to 4 steps for most cold outreach. Short plain emails are also easier on spam filters.
steps.check: Variables show in the editor as placeholders.

steps.do: Add follow-ups with the + button at the bottom and set Wait X days between steps. Leave the follow-up subject empty to reuse the first step's subject.
steps.why: Follow-ups in the same thread usually get more replies than a new thread, and the spacing keeps you polite.
steps.check: Each step shows a wait time.

steps.do: In the editor click Insert Unsubscribe Link, then Insert. Also add your business name and postal address in the signature.
steps.why: Recipients must have an easy way to opt out. US CAN-SPAM also requires a valid postal address.
steps.check: The unsubscribe link and address appear in the preview.

steps.do: Click Preview. Choose a sender in Send From and a lead in Load data for lead, then send a test to your own address.
steps.why: You catch broken variables before 500 people do.
steps.check: The test email arrives and every variable is filled in, not empty.

steps.do: Go to Settings and, under Accounts to use, choose your warmed inboxes.
steps.why: Instantly rotates these inboxes automatically.
steps.check: At least one active inbox is selected.

steps.do: In Schedule & Limits set start date, timezone, sending days (for example During office hours) and a daily limit. Instantly recommends about 30 per sending account per day.
steps.why: A low limit protects your sender reputation.
steps.check: The daily limit equals roughly 30 times the number of inboxes, or lower.

steps.do: In the Settings tab turn on Stop sending emails on reply and Insert Unsubscribe Link Header. Consider Send first email as text-only.
steps.why: Stop on reply avoids emailing someone who answered. The header adds one-click unsubscribe, which the help recommends for compliance and reputation.
steps.check: Those options show as on.

steps.do: Check that leads, variables, saved sequence, test emails, accounts and schedule are all done, then click Launch yourself.
steps.why: You press launch; agents only prepare the CSV and copy.
steps.check: Campaign status changes to active and the first sends appear in Analytics within the schedule window.

mistakes: Uploading an unverified list. High bounces can pause the campaign and hurt your inbox reputation.
Long sequences. The help recommends no more than 3 to 4 steps for most cold outreach.
Empty variables producing emails that start with 'Hi ,'. Preview a lead first, and set Placeholder Values under Advanced Email Body if a field may be blank.
A daily limit too high for new inboxes. About 30 per account is Instantly's example.
Turning on Allow Risky Emails or disabling BounceProtect without a good reason. Both loosen safeguards.
done_when: The campaign is active with sending inboxes assigned.
A test email showed all variables filled and an unsubscribe link.
Daily limit and schedule match your warmed inbox capacity.
recipes.free_alternative: You can prepare the CSV, copy and test sends on the free trial, which allows 2 accounts. Pure planning in a spreadsheet is free.
unverified: The fetched creation article refers to a Settings tab; older guides mention Schedule and Options tabs, so screens may differ slightly by account.
Whether the Insert Unsubscribe Link and the header option are both needed for your region was not stated; using both is the safe choice.

recipes.title: Read Instantly results and fix a campaign
recipes.keywords: instantly analytics results open reply bounce rate fix deliverability auto pause step analytics sending activities
recipes.goal: You can read a campaign's numbers, find the problem (list, inbox or message) and change one thing at a time.
recipes.plan_needed: Not stated on the pages.
before: A campaign that has been sending for at least a few days.
A note of what you launched (list, subject, step 1 text), so you can change one thing at a time.

steps.do: Open the campaign and go to its Analytics tab.
steps.why: This shows the detailed stats for just that campaign.
steps.check: You see sent, replies, bounces and other metrics.

steps.do: Read the key numbers: Total sent, Reply rate (replies divided by total sent), Positive reply rate (opportunities divided by replies) and Opportunities.
steps.why: Replies and opportunities matter more than opens.
steps.check: You can say in one sentence: 'X sent, Y replies, Z opportunities'.

steps.do: Treat open rate carefully. Instantly counts only pixel-tracked opens, so text-only mail clients are not counted.
steps.why: Open numbers are often wrong, and open tracking is switched off if you use text-only delivery optimization.
steps.check: You use reply rate as the main signal.

steps.do: Scroll to Step Analytics to see performance per step and variant.
steps.why: It shows which step gets the replies.
steps.check: You can see which step or variant did best.

steps.do: Check bounces: in the campaign Analytics open Sending Activities and filter by Bounced. You can download the CSV.
steps.why: Bounces are the fastest way to damage a sender reputation.
steps.check: You see the bounced addresses and reasons.

steps.do: If bounces are high, pause, verify the whole lead list again with an email verification tool, remove invalid addresses and remove spam-like words. Instantly says it auto-pauses campaigns when bounces are typically above 5 percent.
steps.why: Cleaning the list is the first fix in Instantly's troubleshooting guide.
steps.check: The re-verified list has fewer risky addresses. After you resume, Instantly will not auto-pause again for 7 days, so watch it yourself.

steps.do: Open the Email Accounts dashboard and check each inbox: connected, not paused, health score, and daily limit not reached.
steps.why: A disconnected or paused inbox quietly stops sending.
steps.check: All inboxes you use show active.

steps.do: If replies are low and bounces are low, change one thing only: the subject line, the first sentence or the offer. Use + Add variant to A/B test.
steps.why: Changing one thing tells you what worked.
steps.check: Step Analytics shows two variants with their own numbers after a few days.

steps.do: Reply to interested people quickly and mark them as opportunities.
steps.why: That feeds the positive reply rate and your own follow-up.
steps.check: Opportunities count rises and the lead moves to your CRM.

mistakes: Changing the list, subject and offer at the same time, so you never learn what worked.
Judging a campaign after one day. Look at several days of data.
Switching off the auto-pause protection to keep sending. Fix the root cause first.
Counting auto-replies as real interest. Auto-replies are included in reply rates by default, and you can turn that off in the gear settings.
done_when: You wrote down this week's numbers and the one change you will test.
Bounce rate is under control and no inbox is paused or disconnected.
Positive replies are in your CRM.
unverified: Instantly gives 5 percent as the typical auto-pause trigger; it is configurable in Preferences and no healthy target rate was stated on the fetched pages.
Menu names were taken from the help pages; the app screen may be slightly different.

recipes.title: Run a multichannel sequence in Lemlist
recipes.keywords: lemlist sequence multichannel linkedin email campaign visit profile invitation sending limits import leads launch
recipes.goal: A lemlist campaign sends an email, then LinkedIn steps for leads who have a LinkedIn URL, within safe daily limits.
recipes.plan_needed: The lemlist help says LinkedIn steps need the Free trial, Multichannel Expert or Enterprise plan, and the Email plan does not include LinkedIn steps. Advanced conditions are also Expert or Enterprise per the search summary.
before: A lemlist account and a connected sending mailbox with SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up.
Your LinkedIn account connected to lemlist (the help also mentions a LinkedIn Chrome extension for some features).
A lead CSV with email and a LinkedIn profile URL for each lead.
A compliance plan: lawful basis, honest identity, and opt-out (see the GTM overview recipe).

steps.do: In the left menu click Campaigns, then Create campaign (top right). Name it after the audience and goal.
steps.why: A clear name helps you find it later.
steps.check: You land on the Sequence tab.

steps.do: Click Add step and build the first email step. Use plain text and a small number of variables.
steps.why: A campaign needs at least one email step before LinkedIn steps can be added.
steps.check: The email step shows in the sequence.

steps.do: Click the email step, open Select senders for your campaign, and choose your mailbox. If lemlist flags a problem click Show errors.
steps.why: The campaign needs a sender to deliver.
steps.check: No sender error is shown.

steps.do: Click Add step, open the Conditions tab and choose Has Linkedin URL.
steps.why: Leads without a profile URL are routed away instead of causing errors.
steps.check: A Yes and a No branch appear.

steps.do: On the Yes branch add Visit profile, then below it add Invitation. Pick the sender and add a short personalised note.
steps.why: A profile visit first looks natural. Invite notes are capped at 200 characters including variables.
steps.check: The steps appear in order with a delay between them.

steps.do: Add an Accepted invite condition and a wait time (the help article recommends 3 to 5 days), then a Chat message step on the accepted branch.
steps.why: Chat messages only reach 1st-degree connections.
steps.check: The branch is complete.

steps.do: Click the Settings (gear) icon and open Schedules & launch. Set sending days, times and the delay between leads.
steps.why: Spacing keeps sending human-like.
steps.check: The schedule is saved.

steps.do: From your profile name (bottom left) open Settings, then Sending limits, and set Maximum number of emails sent by lemlist in 24h for your address. Also check your LinkedIn daily limits there.
steps.why: lemlist's guidance for a mailbox out of warm-up is to start at 10 to 15 emails a day, add about 5 a week and cap at 25 to 30. Warm-up plus campaign should stay at or below 50 per mailbox per day.
steps.check: The limit is set per sending address.

steps.do: Open the Lead list tab and click Import new leads, then choose CSV import and map the columns.
steps.why: Leads need email, first name and a LinkedIn URL for these steps.
steps.check: Leads appear in the list as To Launch.

steps.do: Open the Launch tab, preview a lead's sequence, then click Launch for X leads and confirm with Launch campaign for X leads.
steps.why: You launch it yourself after reviewing.
steps.check: Leads move to Launched. Check the Performance tab later for delivery and replies by step.

mistakes: Using the Email plan and expecting LinkedIn steps to work. They need Multichannel Expert, Enterprise or the trial.
Invite notes over 200 characters.
Sending too many emails from a young mailbox. Stay inside the limits above.
Leads with no LinkedIn URL and no condition, which wastes steps.
Free LinkedIn accounts: the help says only 3 custom-note invites per month, so a free account is not enough for volume.
done_when: The campaign shows leads as Launched.
Sending limits are set and under 30 campaign emails per mailbox per day at the start.
You can see step results in the Performance tab.
recipes.free_alternative: Do the LinkedIn part by hand and use any email tool for the email part. The lemlist free trial lets you try multichannel steps, per the help article.
unverified: Automating LinkedIn may be restricted by LinkedIn's own terms; check them before use. This was not covered by lemlist's pages fetched.
Plan names and prices change; the Advanced conditions plan requirement came from a search summary not a fetched page.
lemlist articles give different daily email numbers; the recipe uses the global daily limit page.

recipes.title: The whole GTM system, start to finish
recipes.keywords: gtm system overview plan outbound process stack start end high level strategy compliance daily volume cold email consent unsubscribe
recipes.goal: You understand the full path from one clear offer to booked calls, and you send cold email safely, legally and at sensible volumes.
recipes.time: about 1 hour to read and plan, then weeks to run
recipes.plan_needed: The method is free to plan. Individual tools (list tools, enrichment, sending tools, domains) have their own plans and prices; check each tool's pricing page.
before: A service you can deliver, and one proof point or sample (a demo labelled as a demo).
A rough idea of who pays for it.
In $0 mode: use only free steps (manual LinkedIn, free tools, planning) until a client pays.

steps.do: Pick one market and one offer: who you help, what problem, what result.
steps.why: A narrow focus makes the message and the list easy.
steps.check: You can say it in one sentence: 'I help [who] get [result] by [how].'

steps.do: Decide the lawful basis before you build the list. US: CAN-SPAM covers business email too, so you need honest sender details, a postal address and an opt-out. UK: PECR lets you email corporate bodies, but sole traders and some partnerships count as individuals and need consent.
steps.why: FTC says each violating email can cost up to $53,088. The ICO says individuals need opt-in consent.
steps.check: You wrote down the rule for each country in your list.

steps.do: Build a small list of people who fit the offer, from sources that allow it: your own research, company websites, public business details, tools used within their terms. Do not buy lists and do not scrape in ways that break a site's terms.
steps.why: Good targeting beats big volume, and lists of unconsented personal data create legal and spam risk.
steps.check: A spreadsheet of 50 to 100 well-fitting companies with a reason each fits.

steps.do: Enrich and verify: find a work email for the right role, then run it through an email verifier before any send.
steps.why: Invalid addresses bounce, and bounces damage your sender reputation. Instantly auto-pauses campaigns when bounces are typically above 5 percent.
steps.check: Each row has a verified email, a first name and one real fact about the company.

steps.do: Set up a separate sending domain and mailboxes, publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and warm up for at least 2 weeks.
steps.why: Google and Yahoo require authentication; Google requires SPF or DKIM for all senders and SPF, DKIM and DMARC for bulk senders (over 5,000 a day).
steps.check: Test email shows SPF and DKIM pass; warm-up health score above 90 in Instantly.

steps.do: Write a short plain-text message: who you are, one specific observation, one easy question. Include your real name, business name, postal address and an unsubscribe option.
steps.why: Honest subject lines and identity are legal rules (CAN-SPAM) and they get better replies too.
steps.check: Under about 100 words, no tricks, no fake 'Re:' subjects.

steps.do: Send slowly from warmed inboxes. Start with about 10 to 15 campaign emails per mailbox per day and move toward 25 to 30. Keep warm-up plus campaign at or below 50 per mailbox per day. Instantly's own example is about 30 per account.
steps.why: These are the vendors' own figures (Instantly and lemlist help pages) and they protect your reputation. More volume should come from more mailboxes and domains, not pushing one mailbox.
steps.check: No mailbox is over its daily limit and bounces stay low.

steps.do: Follow up 2 to 3 times with a few days between, and stop when someone replies or opts out.
steps.why: Most replies come after a follow-up, but pestering raises unsubscribes and complaints.
steps.check: Stop on reply is on; opt-outs are added to a suppression list.

steps.do: Honor opt-outs fast. CAN-SPAM allows up to 10 business days; Yahoo's bulk-sender rule is 2 days, so aim for immediately. Never email an opted-out address again.
steps.why: It is the law and an inbox-provider rule.
steps.check: Your unsubscribe link works and your suppression list is kept.

steps.do: Track every lead in a CRM or simple sheet: sent, replied, call booked, won, lost.
steps.why: You cannot improve what you do not record.
steps.check: Every reply has a status.

steps.do: Watch spam complaints. Google and Yahoo both require spam rate below 0.3 percent; Google's guidance aims for under 0.1 percent. Stop and fix if complaints rise.
steps.why: Crossing 0.3 percent can get your mail blocked.
steps.check: Complaint rate is tracked (Google Postmaster Tools if you send to Gmail in volume) and stays well under limits.

steps.do: Review weekly: replies, bounces, calls booked. Change one thing at a time (list, subject, first line or offer) and write down the result.
steps.why: Learning is the whole system.
steps.check: A notes page with one test per week and its result.

mistakes: Skipping authentication and warm-up and sending big batches on day 1.
Using purchased or scraped personal lists, or ignoring UK consent rules for sole traders.
Hiding who you are, misleading subjects or no unsubscribe option.
Trying to fix low replies by sending more volume instead of improving the offer and list.
Changing many things at once so you cannot tell what worked.
done_when: You have one offer, one list, one message and one compliance checklist.
Your sending domain passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC and the inboxes are warmed.
You track results weekly and test one change at a time.
recipes.free_alternative: In $0 mode do the manual parts: research, writing, LinkedIn by hand, and planning. Buy domains and tools only after the first client pays.
unverified: Steps on offer, list building, enrichment and follow-up cadence are general good practice, not from one official page; the 2 to 3 follow-ups and few-days spacing are a suggestion.
The legal pages cover US CAN-SPAM and UK PECR only. EU/GDPR rules and other countries were not researched; this is not legal advice.
The ICO page says its guidance is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act, so recheck it.

Daily volumes come from Instantly and lemlist help pages (about 30; 10 to 15 rising to 25 to 30; 50 total with warm-up). The numbers differ between articles and are not a guarantee of inbox placement.
The 0.1 percent spam-rate target came from the Google guidance summary; the 0.3 percent limit appears on both Google and Yahoo pages.

recipes.title: Prepare and run a high-ticket sales call
recipes.keywords: sales call closing discovery qualification close script objection follow up spin sandler up-front contract calendly zoom high ticket
recipes.goal: You will run a 30 to 45 minute first call with one simple structure and end it with a clear decision or next step.
recipes.time: 20 minutes prep, then 30 to 45 minutes on the call
recipes.plan_needed: Not a tool task. Calendly plan needs are not covered by the sales sources used here.
before: A booked call (for example through your Calendly link) and the lead's form answers or profile.
The offer's price, what is included, and what is NOT included, written down. Never guess these on a call.
The payment or contract link the offer owner gave you.
A notes document with five headings: Situation, Problem, Cost, Result wanted, Next step.

steps.do: Spend 10 minutes reading the lead's form answers and their website or LinkedIn. Write 3 facts you already know.
steps.why: Research lets you skip basic questions, so the call does not feel like an interview.
steps.check: You have 3 facts written in your notes before the call starts.

steps.do: Open the call with an up-front contract (Sandler method). Say: 'Thanks for jumping on. We have 30 minutes. I would like to ask about where you are now and what you want, then tell you honestly if I can help. At the end, we will decide together: yes, no, or a clear next step. Does that work for you?'
steps.why: You agree on purpose, time, agenda and outcome first, so the lead cannot end the call with 'let me think about it' without a reason.
steps.check: The lead says yes or adjusts the agenda. You both now know how the call ends.

steps.do: Ask Situation questions, but only 2 or 3. Example: 'Tell me what you are doing today to get clients.' and 'How long has it been that way?'
steps.why: SPIN selling starts with facts about their current setup. Too many of these feel like an interrogation, so keep them short.
steps.check: You wrote their current process under Situation.

steps.do: Ask Problem questions. Example: 'What is not working about that?' and 'What have you already tried?'
steps.why: People buy to fix problems they have said out loud, not problems you point out.
steps.check: The lead names at least one problem in their own words. Write their exact words down.

steps.do: Ask Implication questions. Example: 'What does that cost you each month, in money or time?' and 'If nothing changes in 6 months, what happens?'
steps.why: SPIN sources describe this step as the one that makes the problem feel urgent. Beginners skip it most.
steps.check: The lead states a cost, a number, or a consequence. If they cannot, the problem may be too small: be honest and do not push.

steps.do: Ask Need-payoff questions. Example: 'If we fixed that, what would it be worth to you?' and 'What would you do with that result?'
steps.why: The lead says the benefit out loud instead of you claiming it.
steps.check: You have their wanted result in their own words under Result wanted.

steps.do: Qualify before you pitch. Ask: 'Is there a budget set aside for solving this? Who else, if anyone, decides with you?' State the price range early if your offer owner allows it.
steps.why: A good fit has a real problem, the money and the authority to decide. Finding out now saves both sides time.
steps.check: You know yes or no on budget and decision maker. If no, offer a polite end to the call or a later date.

steps.do: Present the offer in 3 parts, using their words: 'You told me [problem], costing [cost], and you want [result]. Here is what we do: [3 to 5 items]. The price is [price]. Based on what you told me, does this fit?' Then stop talking.
steps.why: Tying the offer to their own words keeps it short and relevant. Silence lets them think.
steps.check: The lead answers with a yes, a question, or an objection. You did not fill the silence.

steps.do: Handle an objection with three moves: pause, ask a question, then answer. Example: 'That is fair. Help me understand, is it the price itself or whether it will work for you?' Only make claims the offer owner has approved.
steps.why: The first objection is often not the real one. A question finds the real one.
steps.check: You know the real concern and have answered it honestly, without invented results or fake deadlines.

steps.do: Close by returning to your up-front contract: 'We said we would decide today. Do you want to go ahead?' If yes, send the payment or contract link while still on the call. If no, ask 'What would need to be true for this to be a yes?'
steps.why: You agreed the outcome at the start, so asking for the decision feels fair, not pushy.
steps.check: You end with one of three results: paid or signed, a dated next step, or a clear no.

steps.do: Within 10 minutes after the call, log the result and send a short follow-up: 'Thanks for your time. As discussed: [their problem, in one line], [what we do], next step is [action] by [date]. Reply here if anything is unclear.' Put the follow-up date in your calendar.
steps.why: Fast notes keep details accurate, and a dated next step stops deals from going cold.
steps.check: Your log has the outcome and reason, and the lead has a written summary.

mistakes: Pitching in the first 5 minutes. Run the discovery steps first.
Talking more than the lead. Aim for the lead talking most of the call.
Reading a script word for word. Sandler sources warn that a rehearsed up-front contract creates distance. Use the wording as a guide.
Making income or result promises the offer owner has not approved. Never promise results you cannot prove.
Using fake urgency or pressure. Ask for the decision, but do not trap or rush the lead.
done_when: You opened with an agreed purpose, time and outcome.
You asked at least one Situation, Problem, Implication and Need-payoff question and wrote their answers down.
The call ended with paid, a dated next step, or an honest no.
You logged the result and sent a written follow-up the same day.
recipes.free_alternative: Practise the structure on a free Zoom or Google Meet call with a friend, and record yourself (with their permission) to review your talk time.
unverified: The Sandler 5-element page returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch. Its content was confirmed only through search summaries of several Sandler pages (purpose, time, agendas, outcome).
SPIN example question wording is a beginner adaptation, not quoted from Rackham's book. The Gong guide gave the four categories and cautions, not sample questions.
Rackham's research figures were seen only in secondary sources.
Calendly features and plan limits were not researched here.

recipes.title: Find high-ticket offers that hire closers
recipes.keywords: closer jobs remote commission only high ticket find offers red flags scam pay to play 1099 contract ftc
recipes.goal: You will have a short list of legitimate offers to apply to, a way to check each one, and a clear view of the risks of commission-only work.
recipes.plan_needed: Free to search and apply. A legitimate role should never charge you to apply or work.
before: A one-page summary of your sales practice (calls you have run or role plays).
A notes sheet with columns: company, offer, price of what they sell, commission %, paid when, contract type, red flags.
Understanding that commission-only means you earn only when a sale closes. Income is not guaranteed, and no income is promised here.

steps.do: Understand the usual model before you search. Many remote closer roles are commission-only independent contractor (1099 style) positions: you take sales calls for a coaching, consulting or service company and are paid a percentage of each sale you close. There is often no salary and no benefits.
steps.why: Knowing this stops you being surprised, and it shows which deals are normal and which are not.
steps.check: You can explain in one sentence how you would be paid and when.

steps.do: Search for words like 'closer', 'sales closer', 'enrollment advisor' and 'high ticket sales' on established job boards and on company career pages. Prefer postings that name the company, the product and the pay structure.
steps.why: Real employers show who they are and what they sell. A hidden company name is a warning.
steps.check: You have 5 to 10 postings in your sheet, each with a company name you can search.

steps.do: Also look at LinkedIn Jobs, Upwork and company websites. Message founders with a short, honest note about your skills, rather than answering only anonymous posts.
steps.why: Direct contact with a named owner is easier to verify than a mass ad.
steps.check: At least 3 entries are from a named company with a real website.

steps.do: Check each company. Search its name with the words 'scam', 'review' and 'complaint'. Look for a real website, a named founder, real customers and a registered business.
steps.why: The FTC advises searching the company name with these words before committing any money.
steps.check: You wrote down what you found for each one, including any complaints.

steps.do: Read the pay terms. Ask in writing: What is the commission? When is it paid (on signing, or when the customer pays)? What happens if a customer refunds or cancels? Who handles the contract and payment link?
steps.why: Commission-only deals can hide clawbacks or late payment. You must know them in advance.
steps.check: You have written answers from the company for each question.

steps.do: Ask for a written agreement before doing any calls. It should name both sides, the commission, the payment date, how refunds are treated and how either side can stop working together.
steps.why: No contract means no way to claim money you earned.
steps.check: You hold a signed or accepted written agreement, or you walk away.

steps.do: Apply the red flag list. Walk away if: they ask you to pay for training, a certification, a lead list or access before you can earn. Or they promise big or guaranteed income. Or they pressure you to decide fast. Or they call it a job but it is really a business you must buy. Or they send you a check and ask you to send back part of it.
steps.why: The FTC lists these as typical signs of job and business-opportunity scams. Real employers do not ask you to pay to start.
steps.check: Every offer on your list has a pass or fail against these flags.

steps.do: Ask for proof, not stories. If a company shows earnings numbers, ask what share of people actually reach them, and ask for it in writing. Treat screenshots and testimonials as marketing.
steps.why: The FTC Business Opportunity Rule page says a seller who makes an earnings claim must give a written statement with its source, the period, and the number and percentage of people who got those results.
steps.check: Any earnings claim you saw has either a written statement behind it or you ignored it.

steps.do: Apply to your 2 or 3 best offers with a short message: who you are, 2 sentences on your sales practice, one question about how leads are sourced and qualified. Offer a short trial call.
steps.why: A small, specific message gets answered more than a long one.
steps.check: You sent the messages and logged the date in your sheet.

steps.do: Report a scam if you meet one, at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Do not send money or documents.
steps.why: The FTC asks people to report suspected scams so others are protected.
steps.check: You deleted the contact and logged it as a fail with the reason.

mistakes: Paying for training, a certification or placement to get a closer role. Real employers pay you.
Trusting income screenshots or 'top closer makes $40k a month' claims. These are outliers, not typical results.
Starting calls with no written agreement on commission and payment date.
Applying to coaching and info-product companies without checking them. One guide notes this category has many weak or deceptive offers, including a 2023 FTC action against a closer-training company.
Treating commission-only as a salary. Plan your cash separately and assume you could earn nothing in your first weeks.
done_when: You have at least 5 offers in your sheet, each checked against the red flags.
At least 2 offers have written commission terms and a contract before you start.
You have applied to your top 2 or 3 and logged them.
recipes.free_alternative: Use the free search on LinkedIn Jobs, Upwork and company career pages, and message founders directly.
unverified: How a specific company pays commission varies. Search results showed typical posted structures only, not a verified industry norm.
The remotejobassistant.com article and the 2023 FTC action against a closer-training company were seen in search summaries only, not fetched. Verify on ftc.gov before quoting.
No single official directory of legitimate closer roles exists. The job boards named are general ones and were not individually verified for closer listings.
Whether a 1099 classification is lawful depends on the working arrangement and country. Not researched.

recipes.title: Write and schedule a LinkedIn ghostwritten post
recipes.keywords: linkedin ghostwriting post hook write schedule client voice draft approve clock icon scheduled
recipes.goal: You will have one approved post written in a client's voice, scheduled to publish through LinkedIn's own scheduler.
recipes.plan_needed: The LinkedIn Help page for scheduling personal posts does not state a paid plan requirement.
before: A client who agrees in writing that you draft posts for them.
3 to 5 examples of the client's own writing or a recorded call, to copy their voice.
One topic, one reader, and one thing the reader should do or think after reading.
A decision on who publishes: the client posts and schedules from their own login.

steps.do: Interview the client for 15 minutes. Ask: 'What did you learn this month?', 'What mistake do your customers make?', 'What story would you tell a new customer?'. Record it with permission.
steps.why: Posts that come from real stories are more specific and sound like the client.
steps.check: You have one real story or opinion with a detail (a number, a place, a name you may use).

steps.do: Pick one reader and one point. Write both in one line: 'For [reader], about [point].'
steps.why: One clear point makes the post easier to read and remember.
steps.check: You can say the point in 10 words.

steps.do: Write the hook as one short first line. Good types: a result ('How I ...'), a promise ('How to ...'), a story opener, a surprising fact, or a bold opinion the client truly holds.
steps.why: LinkedIn shows only the first lines before 'see more', so the hook decides whether anyone reads on. This advice comes from creators, not LinkedIn Help.
steps.check: Reading only the first 2 lines, you want to click 'see more'.

steps.do: Write the body in short lines with blank lines between. Use plain words, one idea per line, and a short numbered list if you have steps.
steps.why: White space makes it readable on a phone. LinkedIn Help says a post can hold up to 3,000 characters, so stay well below it.
steps.check: No paragraph is longer than 3 lines.

steps.do: End with one simple question or action. Example: 'What would you add?' Do not stack three asks.
steps.why: A single clear ending invites comments and keeps the post focused.
steps.check: The last line asks one thing.

steps.do: Check the facts and claims. Every number must come from the client. Do not invent results, testimonials or credentials.
steps.why: LinkedIn's Professional Community Policies prohibit false or misleading content and misrepresenting qualifications or achievements.
steps.check: The client confirmed each number and claim.

steps.do: Send the draft to the client for approval in writing. Change the wording until it sounds like them.
steps.why: It is their name and reputation on the post. Approval protects both of you.
steps.check: You have a written 'approved' reply.

steps.do: Have the client put the text into LinkedIn from their OWN login. On desktop, they click 'Start a post' and paste the text. Do not log in as the client or use a shared account.
steps.why: LinkedIn's policies say not to use, create or share accounts for anyone other than yourself. Drafting is fine. Sharing a login is the risk.
steps.check: The text is in the post box on the client's own account.

steps.do: Schedule it. Click the clock icon in the lower-right corner, choose a date and time in the 'Schedule post' window, click Next, then click Schedule. On mobile: tap Post, write, tap the clock icon (upper right), pick the time, tap Next, then Schedule.
steps.why: This is LinkedIn's own scheduler. Times can be from 10 minutes to 3 months ahead and are converted to UTC from the device's time zone setting, so check the zone before you confirm.
steps.check: Clicking the clock icon and 'View all scheduled posts' shows the post with the right date and time.

steps.do: To change it later, open the scheduled list and use the More icon, then 'Modify schedule' or 'Edit post'. To remove it, use the Delete icon and confirm.
steps.why: You can fix mistakes before it goes live.
steps.check: The list shows the updated time, or the post is gone.

steps.do: On the day it publishes, have the client reply to comments for the first hour or two.
steps.why: Real replies build trust. Do not buy likes or arrange to trade likes, which the policies discourage.
steps.check: The client replied to every genuine comment.

mistakes: Logging in as your client or sharing their password. Draft for them, and let them post from their own account.
Burying the point. Put the strongest idea in the first 2 lines.
Inventing numbers, clients or results to make a story stronger.
Scheduling without checking the time zone. LinkedIn converts times using the device's zone setting.
Using bots, engagement pods or auto-comment tools. LinkedIn Help warns posts may have limited visibility if it detects inauthentic activity or automation tools.
done_when: The client approved the final text in writing.
The post shows in the client's scheduled list with the correct date and time.
The client knows to reply to comments when it goes live.
recipes.free_alternative: LinkedIn's built-in scheduler needs no extra tool. Its Help page does not mention a fee.
unverified: Hook, formatting and hashtag advice comes from creator posts in search results, not from LinkedIn official pages. Reach percentages from those posts were not used.
LinkedIn Help page a528176 does not describe formatting, hashtags or mentions, so no step cites it for that.

Whether LinkedIn allows a delegate to post for a personal profile through an official feature was not found. Company Pages have separate admin roles and their own scheduling page (a1419179), not covered here.
The Brand Partnership toggle and other composer options were seen on the Help page but not tested.
